titleStmt.title: A bound for the density of any Hausdorff space

bibl.title: A bound for the density of any Hausdorff space

person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: existence
span.quote: We generalize this result to the class of all Hausdorff spaces by introducing the nonquasiregularity degree nq(X), which is countable when X is quasiregular, and showing d(X) ≤ πχ(X)c(X)nq(X) for any Hausdorff space X.

span.label: density bounds for Hausdorff spaces
span.quote: The density of a topological space X, denoted by d(X), is the least cardinality of a dense subset of X.

span.label: mathematical-proof
span.quote: We prove now the central result in this paper.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: The nonquasiregularity degree simultaneously generalizes quasiregularity and the closed pseudocharacter, so a single inequality in nq(X) specialises to both Šapirovskiĭ's regular-space bound and Sun's Hausdorff bound.
span.quote: This shows that the nonquasiregular degree generalizes both quasiregularity in spaces for which nq(X) is defined and the closed pseudocharacter in Hausdorff spaces.

span.label: The new cardinal function nq(X) is not defined for every topological space, so the main bound does not apply universally.
span.quote: However, there are spaces for which nq(X) is not defined.

span.label: A compact T1 space is exhibited for which the invariant fails to exist.
span.quote: Example 3.4 gives an example of compact, T1 space for which nq(X) is not defined.

span.label: The nq(X) factor cannot simply be dropped: examples are given where the plain bound fails.
span.quote: We give two examples of spaces X where nq(X) is required in our density bound; that is, d(X) > πχ(X)c(X).

span.label: The two classical bounds this paper unifies had complicated proofs that were quite different from one another, which is the gap the paper exists to close.
span.note: what this limits: the relation between Sapirovskii's density bound and Sun's cardinality bound before this paper: Sun's proof is described as a complicated closing-off argument quite different from the proof of the density bound, so the two results were not visibly connected
span.quote: again using a complicated closing-off argument, but quite different than the proof of ˇSapirovski˘ı’s density bound

span.label: The class of spaces the theorem covers is named after the invariant being defined on them, so membership is settled by whether the quantity exists rather than by a topological property.
span.note: what this limits: the scope of the main theorem: it applies to nq-spaces, and a space is an nq-space precisely when nq(X) is defined, which is why a compact T1 example without the invariant falls outside it
span.quote: Definition 2.3. A space X is an nq-space if nq(X) is defined

span.label: density
span.quote: The density of a topological space X, denoted by d(X), is the least cardinality of a dense subset of X

span.label: quasiregular
span.quote: Definition 2.1. A space X is quasiregular if every nonempty open set U of X contains a nonempty open set V

span.label: nonquasiregularity degree
span.quote: introducing the nonquasiregularity degree nq(X), which is countable when X is quasiregular

span.label: nq-space
span.quote: Definition 2.3. A space X is an nq-space if nq(X) is defined

span.label: Hausdorff space
span.quote: We generalize this result to the class of all Hausdorff spaces by introducing the nonquasiregularity degree nq(X), which is countable when X is quasiregular, and showing d(X) ≤ πχ(X)c(X)nq(X) for any Hausdorff space X.

span.label: nonregularity - AS A DEGREE RATHER THAN A DICHOTOMY: instead of a space being regular or not, the paper introduces a cardinal measuring HOW nonquasiregular it is, and the classical bound then holds for every space with that degree as a factor
span.quote: we introduce the nonquasiregular degree nq(X) (Definition 2.2) which gives a “measure” of how nonquasiregular a space is.

span.label: quasiregular - THE HYPOTHESIS WEAKENED ONCE BEFORE IT WAS MEASURED: the classical result was stated for regular spaces, then observed to need only quasiregularity and not even Hausdorff, and only afterwards replaced by a degree
span.quote: It was observed by the author in [1] that this holds if the space has a weaker property called quasiregular (Definition 2.1) and not necessarily even Hausdorff

span.label: the degree - SMALL FOR THE SPACES THAT MATTER: nq(X) is countable when the space is quasiregular and bounded by the closed pseudocharacter when it is Hausdorff, which is what stops the new factor from making the bound vacuous
span.quote: which is countable when X is quasiregular, and showing d(X) ≤ πχ(X)c(X)nq(X) for any Hausdorff space X

span.label: extends → Šapirovskiĭ's density bound d(X) ≤ πχ(X)c(X) for regular spaces
span.quote: We generalize this result to the class of all Hausdorff spaces by introducing the nonquasiregularity degree nq(X), which is countable when X is quasiregular, and showing d(X) ≤ πχ(X)c(X)nq(X) for any Hausdorff space X.

span.label: extends → Sun's bound πχ(X)c(X)ψc(X) for the cardinality of a Hausdorff space
span.quote: This improves Sun’s theorem and shows that the degree to which a space is nonquasiregular plays an important role in the cardinality of a Hausdorff space.

span.label: replicates → Šapirovskiĭ's and Sun's theorems (re-derived from one argument)
span.quote: This results in a unified proof of ˇSapirovski˘ı’s and Sun’s theorems, gives an improved bound for the cardinality of a Hausdorff space, and answers Question 3.3 in [2].

span.label: Hausdorff space —is-a→ nq-space
span.quote: As every Hausdorff space is an nq-space and every quasiregular space is an nq-space

span.label: quasiregular —is-a→ nq-space
span.quote: As every Hausdorff space is an nq-space and every quasiregular space is an nq-space, we have the following corollary

span.label: The density of any space for which the nonquasiregularity degree is defined — in particular every Hausdorff space and every quasiregular space — is at most πχ(X) times c(X) times nq(X).
span.quote: Our main result is that d(X) ≤ πχ(X)c(X)nq(X) for any space X for which nq(X) is defined, including Hausdorff spaces and quasiregular spaces.

span.label: In a Hausdorff space the new cardinal invariant stays small, being bounded above by the closed pseudocharacter.
span.quote: Importantly, if X is Hausdorff then nq(X) is “small” in the sense that nq(X) ≤ ψc(X).

span.label: The single bound yields one common proof of Šapirovskiĭ's density bound for regular spaces and of Sun's cardinality bound πχ(X)c(X)ψc(X) for Hausdorff spaces, which previously had unrelated proofs.
span.quote: This results in a unified proof of both ˇSapirovski˘ı’s density bound for regular spaces and Sun’s bound πχ(X)c(X)ψc(X) for the cardinality of a Hausdorff space X.

span.label: It follows that the cardinality of any Hausdorff space is at most πχ(X)c(X)nq(X)wψc(X), which improves Sun's bound because wψc(X) never exceeds ψc(X) in Hausdorff spaces.
span.quote: A corollary is that |X| ≤ πχ(X)c(X)nq(X)wψc (X) for any Hausdorff space X, where wψc(X) was introduced in [2] and satisfies wψc(X) ≤ ψc(X) if X is Hausdorff.

span.label: The number of regular open sets of an nq-space is likewise bounded by πχ(X)c(X)nq(X).
span.quote: Let X be an nq-space. Then |RO(X)| ≤ πχ(X)c(X)nq(X).

span.label: In a Hausdorff space the nonquasiregularity degree is bounded above by the Lindelöf number.
span.quote: It is also shown that if X is Hausdorff then nq(X) ≤ L(X).

span.label: Hence Lindelöf Hausdorff spaces form a new class, beyond the quasiregular ones, satisfying Šapirovskiĭ's inequality d(X) ≤ πχ(X)c(X).
span.quote: If X is Lindel¨of and Hausdorff then d(X) ≤ πχ(X)c(X).

span.label: Two spaces are exhibited, one of them Urysohn, whose density strictly exceeds πχ(X)c(X), showing the extra factor nq(X) cannot be dropped from the bound.
span.quote: We give two examples of spaces X where nq(X) is required in our density bound; that is, d(X) > πχ(X)c(X). One of these examples is even Urysohn.

span.label: The nonquasiregularity degree is not defined for every space: the cofinite topology on an infinite set is compact and T1 yet has no nq(X).
span.quote: Example 3.4 gives an example of compact, T1 space for which nq(X) is not defined.

span.quote: The density of a topological space X, denoted by d(X), is the least cardinality of a dense subset of X.

span.quote: A space X is an nq-space if nq(X) is defined.

span.label: weak closed pseudocharacter wψc(X)
span.quote: The weak closed pseudocharacter wψc(X) is defined as wψc(X) = sup{wψc(x, X) : x ∈ X}.

span.label: dense closed pseudocharacter dψc(X)
span.quote: The dense closed pseudocharacter dψc(X) of X is defined as the least infinite cardinal κ such that X has a dense set D such that ψc(d, X) ≤ κ for every d ∈ D.

span.label: regular open set
span.quote: Recall a set R in a space X is regular open if R = intR. Let RO(X) denote the set of regular open sets of a space X.

span.label: nq(X) = ℵ0 — For a quasiregular space the nonquasiregularity degree takes its least possible value, the first infinite cardinal — i.e. quasiregular spaces are exactly the 'countably nonquasiregular' ones.
span.quote: In the latter case we have nq(X) = ℵ0.

span.label: χ(X) = 2κ and d(X) > cf (22κ ) > 2κ — In van Douwen's example the character equals 2^κ while the density strictly exceeds 2^κ, so density outruns πχ(X)c(X) and the nq factor is unavoidable.
span.quote: It can be seen that X is Hausdorff, χ(X) = 2κ and d(X) > cf (22κ ) > 2κ.
